Chapter 174: ByteDance Makes Another Big Move

When Chen Guiliang returned to his old hometown, iResearch Consulting Group named China's four major SNS websites.

They were: Xiaonei.com, Zhanzuo.com, Tianji.com, and Ruolin.com.

The first two focused on campus social networking.

The latter two focused on business social networking.

These four were grouped together because they had all received favor from venture capitalists.

On June 5, Xiaonei.com received a $5 million investment. The venture capital firms were IDG and DJ.

On June 21, Ruolin.com received a $5 million investment. The venture capital firms were UCI and SIG.

On June 26, Tianji.com received a $3 million investment. The venture capital firm was Gobi Partners.

On July 5, Zhanzuo.com received a $2 million investment. The venture capital firm was Sequoia Capital.

Zhanzuo.com, which had been crippled by Chen Guiliang, had somehow managed to survive in the cracks. By driving a crazy amount of traffic from Eyou Mail, it now had over 500,000 registered users.

It was unclear why Sequoia Capital had invested in it.

But it wasn't that outrageous. In the other timeline, Zhanzuo.com was ranked third and still got investors. Now, it was only ranked second.

One could only say that Facebook's sky-high valuation in the United States had spurred many investment firms to pour money into China.

Some media outlets exclaimed in alarm that the spring of Web 2.0 had arrived!

At night, Chen Guiliang lay in the courtyard, gazing at the stars.

As he watched, his secretary called. "Mr. Chen, our Kaixin.com is now online."

"Got it," Chen Guiliang said, hanging up.

If it were only Xiaonei.com, there would be no need for ByteDance to grow to a hundred-odd people.

After repeated consideration, Chen Guiliang decided not to follow the "Xiaonei.com → Renren.com" path. Instead, while building Xiaonei.com, he also created a sister website, Kaixin.com.

Xiaonei.com and Kaixin.com had some overlapping functions.

But Kaixin.com allowed anonymous registration, was not limited to the student community, and would also invite celebrities to register for verified accounts.

Besides that, the biggest difference was that Kaixin.com allowed for one-way "following," whereas Xiaonei.com used a mutual friend-adding model.

The one-way "follow" function was technically not difficult at all, but no one in China was doing it at the moment.

This was because the logic of internet socializing at the time emphasized "authentic small-circle interaction" rather than "public sharing and following strangers."

Chen Guiliang wasn't sure if it would succeed, but it was worth a try.

If Kaixin.com was successful, it could pave the way for creating a microblog in the future.

Two months ago, Su Ping graduated from university.

She now used two websites simultaneously.

One was Xiaonei.com, where she could interact with her university classmates.

Although all her classmates had graduated, the class group was still preserved on Xiaonei.com. Whenever she logged into Xiaonei.com, it was as if her class still existed, and her university days hadn't faded away.

The other was Ruolin.com.

It was a website she discovered while job hunting, which had a lot of recruitment information. Many of her current colleagues were also using Ruolin.com.

After a day of work, Su Ping returned to her rented apartment and subconsciously opened Xiaonei.com, wanting to see what updates her old classmates had posted.

And to steal some vegetables on the side.

Then she saw an on-site message: Xiaonei.com's sister website, Kaixin.com, is now live. You can log in with your Xiaonei account and change your nickname at any time, or you can re-register anonymously for a Kaixin account.

Curious, Su Ping clicked the link. An option to change her nickname immediately appeared.

She thought for a moment and changed her Kaixin.com screen name to: Pingping Loves Meat Buns.

Next, she selected her interest tags, choosing literature, food, and entertainment celebrities.

The website then recommended three accounts for her to follow.

One was the famous writer Cheng Cun.

Another was the former food show host Liu Yiwei.

And the other was Super Girl contestant He Jie.

"Wow, there are actually famous people here!" Su Ping quickly followed all of them.

In truth, there weren't many celebrities on the platform yet, mostly relying on Chen Guiliang's personal invitations.

ByteDance had specifically sent people to contact Super Girl contestants, and after much persuasion, managed to get over a dozen to register accounts. Some even made exorbitant demands, saying they would join Kaixin.com only if they were paid a certain amount of money.

Since Kaixin.com had just launched, among the dozen or so Super Girls who had registered, only He Jie and Zhou Bichang had updated their statuses so far, by uploading photos of their daily lives.

Kaixin.com naturally recommended one of them at random.

Su Ping looked everywhere for an "add friend" option, but found that she couldn't add friends, only follow people.

However, there was an address book function. She could add the people she followed to her address book, which was a sort of alternative to adding friends.

Su Ping quickly switched back to Xiaonei.com to chat with her old classmates in their group.

"Has anyone been on Kaixin.com? This website is so strange."

"I checked it out. Six of the top ten Super Girls are on there. I followed all of them. But only He Jie and Zhou Bichang have posted photos so far."

"Where do you find the Super Girls? Kaixin.com only recommended He Jie to me."

"There's a 'More Recommendations' option in the top right corner of the page. Then you can choose category tags, and the corresponding followable accounts will appear."

"What's your nickname? Let's add each other."

A moment later, Su Ping asked, "I can't add you to my address book. It says you haven't followed me."

"So we have to follow each other to be added to the address book. What's your nickname?"

"Pingping Loves Meat Buns."

"Okay, I've followed you. I've already dragged you into my address book."

Chen Guiliang was lying under the starry sky, texting with Bian Guanyue.

The old writer Cheng Cun called him. "Does the number of followers mean the number of my fans?"

"Yes," Chen Guiliang said.

The old man was delighted. "Am I that famous? I've already got over 1,500 followers!"

Chen Guiliang said, "That's because the website automatically recommends you."

"Haha, it's all the same," Cheng Cun said, overjoyed. "I'm hanging up now. I need to hurry and write a little poem to share with my fans."

Limited by technology, internet speed, and costs, Kaixin.com was a bit of a mixed bag.

It couldn't directly repost content, only the title and URL. A user would need the URL to jump to someone else's homepage to comment on their status.

Chen Guiliang wasn't sure if it would be accepted by users.

They were even about to launch a stripped-down microblog function, where users could register their phone numbers to receive text-only status updates of under 70 characters from people they followed. These would be received as SMS messages.

With an MMS-capable phone, you could also receive photos sent by people you followed.

However, the user posting the status update would also have to pay to send out the mini-blog post to be seen via SMS.

But they hadn't finalized the deal with China Mobile yet.

Because if someone had too many followers, under China Mobile's current charging model, the average user simply couldn't afford it. For example, Mobile QQ charged 0.1 yuan for every message received.

ByteDance was currently negotiating a monthly subscription plan with China Mobile, hoping that users could pay 5 yuan a month to receive unlimited Kaixin.com text messages. But it was estimated to be a difficult negotiation, and the final plan might be at least 10 yuan a month.

Additionally, users could also choose to receive messages from only some of the people they followed. Otherwise, if a user followed too many people, the SMS bombardment would be unbearable.

This was a brand new attempt.

Next year, a similar thing would emerge in the United States, also using SMS to receive status updates. It would be called a mini-blog, a prototype of the microblog.

One shouldn't think of SMS as annoying. In this era, people would scroll through and read every single text message.

As long as they could secure the partnership with China Mobile and grow Kaixin.com's user base, this thing would become ByteDance's most profitable cash cow.

The day after Kaixin.com went online.

Yang Shuqi, an employee ByteDance had hired in June, arrived at Tangren Media in the Magic City.

"Have all of Tangren Media's actors join Kaixin.com as a group?" Karen Tsoi didn't understand the point.

Yang Shuqi said, "CEO Tsoi, this is the internet era. Online promotion is just as important as print media promotion. With print media, you have to go through an intermediary, but online, celebrities can face their fans directly."

Karen Tsoi asked, "Our company's artists get paid to appear on shows. How much does your company plan to pay?"

"We can help drive traffic to Tangren's celebrities. When new users register, we can randomly recommend they follow Tangren's stars," Yang Shuqi said. "Kaixin.com is still in its startup phase right now. In the future, when our user base grows to several million, if celebrities still want to be recommended for follows, we'll be charging for that."

Karen Tsoi let out a laugh, half in amusement, half in disbelief. "So celebrities have to pay you to be on your website?"

"Yes," Yang Shuqi said. "The Super Girls are hot right now, aren't they? More than ten of them have already joined Kaixin.com, including six from the top ten. The other four were turned down by us flatly because they wanted money."

"In the future, we'll also partner with China Mobile. A celebrity just has to send a status update of a few dozen words, saying when their new TV series is going to air, and the fans following them will immediately receive it as a text message. Think about how much that would save in promotional fees."

"Even Tangren Media itself can create an account on Kaixin.com in the company's name to release information about new dramas."

These last few sentences piqued Karen Tsoi's interest. "How many users does your website have now?"

Yang Shuqi replied, "Kaixin.com went online at 8 p.m. last night. As of now, we have over 120,000 users."

Many of these 120,000 users were directed from Xiaonei.com.

But quite a few also came from Tieba and forums. Especially the Super Girl Baidu Tieba; a few posts were made, and when the members heard that the Super Girls had joined Kaixin.com, they swarmed over to register accounts.

Karen Tsoi was astonished. Over 120,000 users in less than a day?

She quickly recognized the business opportunity in this.

Yang Shuqi continued, "Your company's celebrities can post their own photos and write their own articles. If they're too busy, their agents can manage it for them. It won't take up the celebrities' time."

"Let me take a look at your website first," Karen Tsoi said.

Half an hour later, ByteDance and Tangren Media reached a cooperation agreement.

The moment Yang Shuqi stepped out of the elevator, he called the company. "It's settled. Not only are Tangren's celebrities willing to join, but the company also registered an account."

Xie Yang said, "Well done. I'll arrange for verification and assign people to post and promote it right away. With Hu Ge and the others, our user numbers will surge again."

"I'm heading to the next company tomorrow," Yang Shuqi said.

Xie Yang replied, "When you get back, we'll celebrate your success!"

Kaixin.com, as much of a mixed bag as Chen Guiliang had made it, had the potential to detonate like a nuclear bomb in the summer of 2005.

You have to remember, at this time, not even blogs were actively inviting celebrities yet.

Sina Blog was still more than two months away from its launch. Only then would it start actively inviting celebrities to join. The moment the celebrities arrived, they would crush all the other blogs at once!

And Kaixin.com not only had a journal for long-form blog posts, but also a stripped-down microblog function that could use China Mobile to send short text message updates.

If I didn't read the chapter comments, I would have always thought the enlistment age was 16. Because three of my middle school classmates joined the army at 16. I also have a younger cousin who joined at 17...

(End of this chapter)
